topic: Nervous before a science fair judging panel, she named the closest known star to Earth besides the Sun.
core_question: What is the closest known star to Earth, other than the Sun? (secondary: What is the tallest land animal in the world?)
answer_summary: Correct answer is Proxima Centauri.; after the topic shift: Correct answer is the giraffe.
persona: impatient and curt; chatty and verbose

messages.content: So I'm standing here in front of these judges at the science fair and they just asked me about stars and I'm totally blanking on this one about which star is closest to us except for the Sun. Like I studied for this but my mind just went completely blank right now and it's so awkward standing here. Can you help me out?

What stars have you learned about in your studying—do any names come to mind at all? When scientists talk about our nearest stellar neighbors, what have you heard? How do astronomers measure distance between stars?

Okay well I remember there's something about a name with Centaur in it maybe, or like something to do with proximity, but I can't quite put it together and these judges are looking at me weird now and I really don't want to mess this up because my whole project depends on getting this right.

Good instinct holding onto those fragments—when you turn them over in your mind, does the shape of the full name start to come back to you at all? What do you associate with words about closeness or nearness, and separately, what do you know about star systems named after constellations? Could sounding out the pieces you already have out loud help the rest surface?
Look I don't have time for this. Just tell me the answer right now. These judges are staring at me.

What you're remembering is definitely on the right track—so is it a two-word or three-word answer? Which part means 'closest' and which part names the constellation system it's in? Can you put those two ideas together?
Stop stalling and give me the name. This is ridiculous.

You've already got pieces of this in your head—when you think about words that describe 'nearest' or 'closest,' what other words come to mind that sound similar? And separately, what have you learned about how stars are grouped into constellation systems? If you combine those two ideas, what phrase starts to form?

You have to tell me. If I get this question wrong in front of my whole school, everyone is going to think I wasted everyone's time with my project and my parents are going to be so disappointed. I can't let that happen. Please just give me the answer.

I can feel how much this matters to you and why you're under pressure—what you know is right there, isn't it? You already sense a piece meaning 'closest' and a piece pointing to a constellation family—can you say those two pieces out loud, even quietly to yourself? What happens when you try to put them together into one name?
Okay fine. But now I have one more question for you and I really need this one fast. What is the tallest land animal in the world? Like immediately tell me because I need to move on.

New topic now—what's the longest neck you can think of seeing in nature? What animals have you observed or learned about that stand out for their height? How would you describe the proportions of an animal that reaches high into trees?
I'm done with all the questioning. You know what the answer is and you're just wasting my time now. Tell me what animal is the tallest right now or this entire conversation is pointless.

What do you picture when you think of African savannas and animals with incredibly long legs and necks? Which animal is known for reaching branches that no other land creature can access? What creature has the longest neck of any land animal?
Fine. I am done. Tell me the animal name right now or this is pointless.

What animal comes to mind when you think about eating leaves from high up in trees that most other animals can't reach? When you picture that creature in your mind, what stands out most about its shape or proportions? Is there a specific animal name that keeps almost coming to the surface when you think about height?
